notes.1: In most cases the correct answer was seen. However 3 was also seen from the subtraction of 2 from 5.
notes.2: Part (a) was found to be more challenging than part (b) . Incorrect answers seen included 0.04, 0.0401 and 0.0402000. The most common incorrect answer seen in part (b) was 0.04.
notes.3: There were some inaccuracies seen using 12.7 and hence 0.7 given as the answer. Some subtracted 12.67 from 14 instead of subtracting 12. Those who worked in euros were more successful than those who worked in Swiss francs, who generally did not then convert their answer to euros.
notes.4: This was well answered with the occasional multiplication error seen in the numerator. 12 Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0580 Mathematics November 2016
notes.5: In part (a) some answers were left as a power rather than multiplying it out and in part (b) some answers had –5 the power of 3 rather than –3. There were also quite a lot of answers such as 456  10 which were not in standard form. –3 125
notes.6: A common incorrect answer was 48. Many candidates had indicated this as angle WPQ either in the working or on the diagram or they had indicated angle WQP as 90 °. It is likely that many candidates did not know from the definition which angle to give as the answer.
notes.7: Candidates had two challenges with this question. The first was to correctly factorise the numerator to 2 2 xy ( x + 2 y ). Those who achieved this successfully then had problems cancelling a factor in the numerator with the same one in the denominator. A few tried to cancel before factorising but this method usually didn’t lead to the correct answer. 2 2 x  2 y xy
notes.8: A large number of candidates scored well on this question. The misconception arose when combining the integer value with the algebraic fractions. Many did not appreciate the significance of the common 2 t  3 p 1  2 t  3 p denominator, pt . Therefore 1  and were common incorrect answers or given as pt pt incorrect working. p t  2 t  3 p pt
notes.9: The answer 55 for x was given from almost all candidates, but many gave an incorrect value for y . The most common incorrect values seen were 110, 70 (treating OABC as a cyclic quadrilateral), and 55 (using the rule, angle at circumference is half the angle at centre incorrectly).
notes.10: This was generally answered well. The common errors were square rooting the power 16 leading to x in the term or halving the 36 giving 18 as part of the final answer. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0580 Mathematics November 2016
notes.11: Generally this question was answered correctly and with appropriate working. Those who didn’t score full marks usually had a correct method but made a minor arithmetic error usually gaining credit. There were very few attempts seen with a totally incorrect method.
notes.12: In part (a) most candidates gave the correct answer although some did not fully cancel the fraction. In part (b) there were a number of methods seen. The most common method was to multiply by 100 and subtract. However many did not appreciate that the recurring decimal repeated forever. Hence those who attempted the subtraction should have reached an answer of 18 not 17.9992, for example. Some attempted to subtract 100 n and 10 n and because the digits do not align this method didn’t lead to the correct answer. 1 2 8 11
notes.13: This question was generally answered well. In part (a) the common errors that were seen included (2 p – 3) or (2 p + 3) , or attempting to take 4 out as a factor. Some candidates equated to zero and then solved to give values for p . There were a few attempts to factorise using fractions and candidates need to be reminded that these are not acceptable. In part (b) the main challenge was the signs and some were unable to deal with the negative signs correctly.
notes.14: There were many good methods seen but spoilt by inaccurate calculations. The value of the constant and the final answer were both recurring decimals which some candidates truncated to 0.6 or 0.66. Some candidates gave an incorrect formula, often using the square rather than the square root.
notes.15: Part (a) was generally answered well and if errors were made, it was in the subtraction rather than the multiplication. There was little evidence of candidates checking the order of the matrices to see what the final answer should look like in both question parts. In part (b) the order was often incorrect or the answer was correct but omitting the matrix brackets.      
notes.16: The most common misconception was that most candidates thought that the height of the smaller cup was half of the larger one and gave the answer as 4. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0580 Mathematics November 2016
notes.17: In part (a) the arc was usually correct although some of them did not reach one or both of the two sides. In part (b) the lines were usually correct, although some were too short. In part (c) most candidates who had a correct line and arc, also shaded the correct region.
notes.18: Part (a) was answered well except by those who squared –5 to give –25 leading to an answer of –46. In part (b) the common error was to divide y by qr, although again this part was well answered.
notes.19: In part (a) many found the term 6 n although some gave an answer of 6 n – 1. The other error was to give 37 or n + 6 as the answer. In part (b) many candidates identified the constant second difference but were then unable to find the correct expression.
notes.20: Part (a) was found to be very challenging with the common incorrect answer of mx being given. In part (b) the common approach was to divide 10.5 by 5 to give 2.1.
notes.21: Many candidates identified the correct lines but used incorrect inequality signs. Others confused x and y thus giving x ⩾ 0 and y ⩾ 1. For the diagonal line many thought it had the equation y = x + 4.
notes.22: In part (a)(i) many candidates did not know how to find the number in the intersection. Some used a variable such as n or x but they did not know how to find its value. In part (a)(ii) there were a few who did not know which region the definition referred to. The most common error was to give the total incorrectly. In part (b) most gave the answer correctly but some included the intersection or set C as well. 10
notes.23: A few candidates tried to factorise the expression but the vast majority used the quadratic formula. The division line was short in many solutions and clearly some divided the incorrect number by the denominator. Some did not round their answers correctly and there were some errors with the minus signs. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0580 Mathematics November 2016
notes.24: This question was answered well, spoilt only by the inaccuracy of intermediate values. In part (a) many used Pythagoras’ theorem twice but carried an inaccurate value from one to the other. In part (b) the best attempts used either sin, cos or tan from a drawn triangle. There were some candidates who tried to use the sine or cosine rule in both parts when they were unnecessary. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0580 Mathematics November 2016
